| [LIT-002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-002.md) v2 | Nested Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes | Paisley et al. (2012), [ARXIV-1210.6738](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.6738). The nHDP gives each document its own DP over the children of every node of a shared global nCRP tree (G_i^(d) ~ DP(βG_i)), plus a per-node stop/continue switch U_{d,i} ~ Beta(γ1, γ2). Each word then takes its own path, and β → 0 recovers the single-path nCRP. The paper fits this with SVI plus a greedy per-document subtree selection. On small corpora the variational nHDP beats variational nCRP on all three datasets and Gibbs nCRP on two of three (PNAS −6.304 vs −6.496/−6.574 held-out log-likelihood). | [LIT-003](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-003.md) v2 | A structure theorem for generalized-noncontextual ontological models | Schmid et al. | [LIT-007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-007.md) v2 | Quasi-quantization: classical statistical theories with an epistemic restriction | Spekkens (2014), [ARXIV-1409.5041](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.5041). Take a classical statistical theory over a phase space Ω = R^{2n} or (Z_d)^{2n}, and allow only uniform distributions over V^⊥ + v, where V is an isotropic subspace (a Poisson-commuting set of linear "quadrature" variables) and v ∈ V gives their values. The result is operationally identical to the quadrature quantum subtheory (the stabilizer formalism for odd prime d) for continuous variables and for odd prime d; the proof is that the Wigner functions of that subtheory are exactly these distributions (§IV.A). For d = 2 the two theories are isomorphic element by element but make different predictions, because the qubit stabilizer subtheory is contextual (§IV.B). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-013); the clearest single statement of the epistricted-theory programme, and the source of the weak/strong nonclassicality split that 2111.13727 and 2005.07161 build on; read it for §II–IV and App. A, not for Table II, which it asserts rather than derives. |

| [LIT-019](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-019.md) v2 | Why interference phenomena do not capture the essence of quantum theory | Catani et al. (2021), [ARXIV-2111.13727](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13727). The paper models each mode of the interferometer as a classical bit pair (occupation N ∈ Z_2, phase Φ ∈ Z_2). The agent may know only one of N, Φ or N⊕Φ and must be maximally ignorant of the rest. Under that restriction, local and deterministic dynamics (beamsplitter: swap N_L with Φ_L⊕Φ_R) reproduce exactly the 50-50, ϕ ∈ {0, π} Mach–Zehnder statistics (output port L with probability 1 or 0; ½/½ with a which-way detector). The same holds for the Elitzur–Vaidman bomb tester (success probability ¼), delayed choice and the quantum eraser (interference within each P_A outcome class, none within each Q_A class). So this "TRAP" slice of interference phenomenology cannot, on its own, force wave–particle complementarity, observer-dependence or nonlocal/retrocausal influence. The paper leaves aside the phenomenology it concedes is nonclassical (unbalanced beamsplitters, the functional form of the duality relation, Hardy's interferometer). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-018); It is the worked, experiment-by-experiment defence of placing interference in the weakly nonclassical column of LIT-007's Table II, and it has the clearest statement of the Spekkens-school methodology (define classicality, formalize it, prove a no-go). Read §3, §4.3, §5.1 and App. A. Its noncontextuality claim for the toy field theory is asserted, not proved. |

An editorial review with no new result. Its one formal item (§4, Eq. 4.1: x(t+1) = f[x(t)], x(0) = x₀) sorts phenomena three ways. Non-emergent: local rules plus initial conditions let you deduce the "expected" high-level pattern. Weakly emergent: they let you deduce an "unexpected" one by computation. Strongly emergent: no deduction is possible even in principle. "Unexpected" is never defined. The rest is a cross-domain survey (§3), a 16-paper map of the theme issue (§5), and an outlook (§6). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-007); worth reading as the table of contents and framing of the Phil. If N entities' resources follow GBM (drift μ, volatility σ, independent noise), then pooling and sharing equally every step leaves the drift at μ, cuts the volatility to σ/√N (Eq. 3.9), and raises each member's time-average growth rate from μ − σ²/2 to μ − σ²/(2N) (Eq. 4.1). The premium is (σ²/2)(1 − 1/N) (Eq. 4.2). The homogeneous state is unstable exactly when the species are self-attracting, μ(p) − μ(s) < 0 (Eq. 6). The paper argues philosophically, not formally, that the quantum theory of open systems "GT" is more fundamental than standard closed-system quantum theory "ST". GT treats states as density operators that evolve, in general, non-unitarily, and it admits not-completely-positive maps. The ontic and epistemic cases each win only on a second, interpretation- or practice-laden criterion: OntFund-2 and EpFund-2. On the first, formal criteria (OntFund-1, EpFund-1) the two frameworks tie, and the authors say so because Stinespring dilation and dropping the Lindblad terms translate in both directions (§4.1, §4.2.1). Explanatory fundamentality is granted only deflationarily (ExFund-1), and the authors recommend dropping the notion (§4.2.2). The step from there to "the open systems view is fundamental tout court" (§4.3) rests on the special sciences and on "there are no other options". | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-077); worth reading as the clearest statement of the "open systems view" and of the distinction between a view, a framework, a theory and a model (§2, §4.1, §5.2). It defines the environment's work capacity C_work = max over agent models of ⟨H(A_t\|M_t) − H(S_t\|M_t)⟩_t (in k_BT ln 2 per round) and proves two things. First, for unifilar environments whose percepts ignore actions, the efficient agents are exactly the randomize-and-forget ∩ maximally-predictive ones, and C_work = log\|A\| − h(S). | [LIT-042](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-042.md) v2 | Shannon invariants: A scalable approach to information decomposition | Gutknecht et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2504.15779](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15779). For any set of quantities Π(α) satisfying the PID consistency equation (A7), whatever the redundancy measure, two averages are fixed by Shannon quantities alone. They are the average degree of redundancy, r̄ = Σᵢ I(Xᵢ;Y)/I(X;Y) (Prop. 1), and the average degree of vulnerability, v̄ = Σⱼ I(Xⱼ;Y\|X₋ⱼ)/I(X;Y) (Prop. 2). Two identities follow: RSI = (r̄ − 1)·I(X;Y) (Cor. 1), and a new "dual" index DRSI = I(X;Y) − Σⱼ I(Xⱼ;Y\|X₋ⱼ) = (1 − v̄)·I(X;Y) (Prop. 4, Cor. 2). In small, stochastically quantised (8-level) networks analysed on their own training set, r̄ about the label rises with depth and v̄ falls with depth and training. In a face autoencoder, decoder layers are more redundant than size-matched encoder layers, and r̄ rises with bottleneck width. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-045); the theory (§II–III, App. B) is short, correct and redundancy-measure-free. | [LIT-044](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-044.md) v2 | The Epic Story of Maximum Likelihood | Stigler (2007), [ARXIV-0804.2996](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.2996). Stigler gives a history of maximum likelihood from Lagrange (1769) to Le Cam (1953). Fisher gave three optimality arguments. The 1922 one rests on the false belief that ML estimates are always sufficient. The 1925 "ANOVA" one derives the information inequality V ≥ 1/I(θ) from Var X = E Var(X\|T) + Var E(X\|T), treating approximate normality as exact. The third, sent privately to Hotelling in 1930, holds for multinomial models and smooth degree-0-homogeneous estimators, and was published only in disguise in 1935. Stigler's verdict is that the Neyman–Scott growing-parameter example (Wald 1938, published 1948) is the practically important failure. He calls Hodges's 1951 superefficiency example "an ingenious but minor technical achievement", because the superefficiency set has Lebesgue measure zero (Le Cam 1953). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-074); an authoritative, archive-based history by the leading historian of statistics, and worth reading for exactly which ML optimality claims were proved, under what conditions, and which counterexamples matter. It is a history, not a technical reference: for modern conditions it points to Bahadur (1964), Le Cam (1953, 1990), van der Vaart (1998) and Cox (2006). |
| [LIT-045](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-045.md) v5 | Structural Realism | Ladyman (2007), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/structural-realism/>. The entry presents structural realism (Worrall 1989) as the attempt to keep both the no-miracles argument and the lesson of theory change. What is retained, and what we are entitled to believe, is structure, understood by ontic structuralists as modal structure. It sorts the view into an epistemic form, which falls to the Newman/Demopoulos–Friedman triviality result when stated as a Ramsey sentence (§3.2), and an ontic form with seven distinguishable theses, from eliminativism about individuals to "objects are constructs" (§4). The ontic form is motivated by quantum non-individuality and entanglement, gauge symmetry and the hole argument. The entry closes with seven objections, each answered in the author's own voice (§5). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-038.md)); the standard map of the structural-realism literature, written by the founder of OSR. For finite-state chains the ordinary plug-in estimator is exactly this estimator, with d = (a−1)a^k(b^k−1). For a linear Gaussian VAR, T̂ is half the Granger-causality statistic. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-053); a short, correct letter and the standard citation for reading transfer entropy as a log-likelihood ratio. | [LIT-053](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-053.md) v2 | The Homological Nature of Entropy | Baudot & Bennequin (2015), DOI-10.3390/e17053253. On a finite probability space, take an information structure S (a set of partitions closed under joins that have a common refinement in S and containing the trivial partition) and a probability family Q complete for it. The information cohomology H*(S;Q) is computed by a Hochschild-type bar complex whose action is Shannon's averaged conditioning. If S is connected and "sufficiently rich" and cochains are measurable, then H¹ is one-dimensional and spanned by Shannon entropy (Thm 1). This makes entropy the unique measurable 1-cocycle, up to one multiplicative constant per connected component. In the unitary-invariant quantum case H¹_U = 0: Shannon entropy is the coboundary of minus the von Neumann entropy, which is the unique invariant 0-cochain with that property up to an additive constant (Thm 3). The tree ("arborescent") version again gives H¹ spanned by entropy (Thm 4). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-088](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-088.md)); the founding paper of information cohomology, with complete proofs of the degree-one results (Thms 1, 3, 4). Reduction elsewhere moves away from a point of view toward the objective; here that move leads away from the thing being explained. So physicalism may be true, but we have no conception of how it could be. He then argues that ψ describes random discontinuous motion (RDM) of N point particles in 3-space: \|ψ\|² is the density with which each particle is present at each instant, and ψ is a single-case propensity. For theories with ideal existence, uniqueness and a dynamical time-translation group, time is three intertwined ℝ-actions (on spacetime, on the symplectic space of solutions, and on the isomorphic space of initial data), and change is a slicing-indexed family of functions on those spaces. Singular dynamics, gauge freedom and time-dependence each damage this picture in a repairable way. Spatially compact vacuum GR breaks it, because the reduced Hamiltonian vanishes (h ≡ 0) and there is only one canonical isomorphism between the reduced spaces. That is the problem of time. It is not an artefact of the 3+1 split, it does not show change to be illusory, and it is absent from asymptotically flat GR and from artificially generally covariant theories. A parameterized "geometric time", such as CMC, restores change and, in the CMC case, a time-dependent Hamiltonian flow. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-118](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-118.md)); worth reading as the careful technical-philosophical statement of what the problem of time is and is not in classical GR. Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). The chapter argues by analogy that deep neural networks are "stochastic measuring devices". The trained weights are a model, and generation is simulation. DNNs are stochastic because random initialisation and non-convex loss mean runs need not converge to the same weights, failing Baird's "regularity" condition. The problems of interpreting model states and generated text are therefore the familiar problems of instruments, models and simulations. The paper proposes a definition, (MSC). A mathematical structure S = ((A_i), (S_j)) is a structure *of* conscious experience iff (S1) its domains are sets of experiential aspects, and (S2) every relation or function S_j has an "S_j-aspect". An S_j-aspect is an aspect that a variation of experience changes exactly when the variation fails to preserve S_j. The older condition (MDC), that a structure is "of" experience if its domains are aspects and its axioms hold, survives only as the necessary condition for *describing* experience, because as a sufficient condition it admits incompatible structures (discrete and non-discrete topologies on the same set), arbitrary re-definitions (every C·d for C > 0) and consciousness-indifferent structures. Lossless compression of trained-model files works almost entirely through the float exponent. It is concentrated on about 40 of 256 values, the top 12 hold ~99.9% of parameters, and it compresses to ~33% under order-0 Huffman coding, while sign and mantissa stay ≈100%. So "regular" BF16 models compress to ~66.4% and FP32 models to ~83%. Rounded "clean" models reach 33.7–48.1%, and ZipNN (exponent extraction plus Huffman only) beats vanilla Zstd by 17% in size and 62% in single-thread speed on Llama-3.1-8B BF16. Damasio (1997), DOI-10.1126/science.275.5304.1293. In the four-deck gambling task, 10 controls and 6 ventromedial prefrontal patients were tracked on choices, anticipatory skin-conductance responses and verbal reports. All controls and no patients developed anticipatory responses; controls came to prefer the good decks, significantly from the point they reported a hunch; three patients who could state the correct strategy kept choosing the bad decks. The authors conclude that nonconscious biases guide behaviour before conscious knowledge does. The statistics support the group difference more firmly than the "before knowing" timing. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-331.md)); worth reading as the experiment the somatic marker hypothesis is usually cited for, and worth reading with its notes, which are weaker than its abstract. With 10 controls and 6 ventromedial patients, the robust results are that every control and no patient developed anticipatory skin-conductance responses, and that three patients who could state the right strategy still chose badly. The headline that controls chose well and responded to risky decks "before they knew" is only partly carried by the statistics: in the pre-hunch period the controls' preference for the good decks was not significant (note 9), and the reported SCR effect there is a group-by-period interaction, not a bad-versus-good-deck difference (note 8). Controls chose the good decks significantly only once they reported a hunch. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |
| [LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md) | The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | Damasio (1996), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1996.0125. States the somatic marker hypothesis: ventromedial prefrontal cortex holds learned links between classes of situation and the body states (emotions) that went with them; when a situation recurs, those states are re-enacted, through the body or through an "as if" loop in somatosensory cortex, and mark imagined option-outcome pairs as good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, so that reasoning works over a pruned space. Evidence summarised: ventromedial patients with intact intellect decide badly in life, lack skin-conductance responses to emotive pictures, and in the gambling task keep choosing the losing decks and show no anticipatory responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the somatic marker hypothesis by its author, with the evidence it then rested on. It is a hypothesis paper: the mechanism (ventromedial prefrontal linkages that re-enact body states, by a "body loop" or an "as if body loop", which then mark options good or bad) is stated, not shown, and the evidence it reports is lesion and skin-conductance work summarised from other papers, without numbers. Its strongest piece, that ventromedial patients lack anticipatory skin-conductance responses in the gambling task while responding normally to the losses themselves, is reported here in one paragraph; the 1997 Science report filed alongside it is the place to see that result. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |
| [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md) | The nature of feelings: evolutionary and neurobiological origins | Damasio & Carvalho (2013), Nature Reviews Neuroscience 14:143–152. Feelings are mental experiences of body states, and they report homeostatic value: a valenced read-out of interoceptive maps that lets an organism learn and anticipate what restores or threatens its physiology. The first integrated whole-body maps are in the upper brainstem (parabrachial nucleus, periaqueductal grey, deep superior colliculus); the insula refines feeling but is not needed for it, since a patient with both insulae destroyed still feels pain, pleasure, hunger and compassion. The authors propose, without evidence of their own, that feeling starts in unmyelinated interoceptive fibres open to ions and ligands along their length. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-330](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-330.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of Damasio's account of feeling as the felt read-out of homeostatic body maps, with its two empirical planks: patients whose insulae are destroyed still feel, and the upper brainstem is where whole-body interoceptive maps first assemble. It is an Opinion piece with no new data. The systems-level case rests on lesion and stimulation evidence it cites; the cellular proposal (unmyelinated interoceptive fibres and ephaptic coupling as the root of sentience) is offered as a hypothesis and stays one. |
| [LIT-389](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-389.md) v2 | Some Possible Roles for Topos Theory in Quantum Theory and Quantum Gravity | Isham & Butterfield (1999), arXiv:gr-qc/9910005. Isham & Butterfield argue, without proving anything new, that presheaf toposes over a base of "contexts" suit physics because the subobject classifier Ω is fixed by the base. They say this answers the objection that many-valued logics are arbitrary (§2.2), and that it keeps the logic distributive (§1.1). They then sketch seven applications. Five are speculative one-paragraph proposals (frames, observers, causal sets, TQFT, synthetic-differential-geometry time in continuous histories). One (§3.7) recaps their Kochen–Specker results: KS ⇔ the dual presheaf D(Â) = Hom(W_A, {0,1}) on the operator category O has no global sections (dim H > 2), and every state ψ gives a FUNC-obeying sieve-valued valuation ν^ψ(A ∈ Δ) = {f_O : Â → B̂ \| Ê[B ∈ f(Δ)]ψ = ψ}. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-334](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-334.md)); worth reading only as the programme's short, informal manifesto as of 1999, written before parts III–IV appeared. It joins the Kochen–Specker valuations to the continuum scepticism (real-valued quantities, space and probabilities) that the Döring–Isham programme later develops, and the Literalism/Extra-Values framing appears nowhere else in the record. Its one technical section is a recap of KS I–II, and a reader of [LIT-325](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-325.md), [LIT-381](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-381.md) and [LIT-378](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-378.md) loses little by skipping it. |
| [LIT-390](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-390.md) v2 | Topos Theory and Consistent Histories: The Internal Logic of the Set of All Consistent Sets | Isham (1996), arXiv:gr-qc/9607069. Isham takes the poset B of all Boolean subalgebras ("windows") of the history orthoalgebra UP, ordered by coarse-graining, and shows that the presheaf A_d(W) = {α \| some d-consistent W′ ⊇ W contains α} is a subobject of the constant presheaf ΔUP, whereas the naive "realisable in W" assignment is not a presheaf at all (§4.1–4.2). The probability claim ⟨α, p⟩ then gets the sieve-valued semantic value {W ⊆ W₀ \| ∃ d-consistent W′ ⊇ W with α ∈ W′} if d(α, α) = p and ∅ otherwise (4.16), a global element 1 → Ω in Set^B, so the logic of "all consistent sets at once" is the distributive but non-Boolean Heyting algebra of sieves on B. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-333](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-333.md)); worth reading as the origin of the Isham school's sieve-valued, coarse-graining truth values, which the Kochen–Specker series names as its motivation (KS I, ref. [13]); it is the only place the construction is applied to consistent histories, it is short and elementary, and its constructions are correct as stated, but read it knowing that the Heyting values measure only whether α can be embedded in a consistent set (the probability d(α, α) is the same in every window), so it says nothing about the conflicts between consistent sets that motivate it. |
| [LIT-392](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-392.md) | Absent Qualia, Fading Qualia, Dancing Qualia | Chalmers (1995), in T. Metzinger (ed.), Conscious Experience (Imprint Academic, co-published in Paderborn). Principle: any system with the same fine-grained functional organisation as a conscious system has qualitatively identical experiences. Replace neurons gradually with silicon chips that keep the organisation. If the end point lacked experience, a midpoint would be a rational being wrong about all its experience ("fading qualia"). If it differed in experience, a switch between two circuits would flip experience with no possible noticing ("dancing qualia"). Both are judged implausible, so absent and inverted qualia are nomologically impossible. The argument extends explicitly to a population of homunculi. The result is "nonreductive functionalism": organisation fixes experience with natural, not metaphysical, necessity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-347](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-347.md)); worth reading as the full statement of the principle of organizational invariance and the fading- and dancing-qualia arguments for it. Cite it carefully: the principle is conditional on fine-grained functional isomorphism to a system already conscious. It covers silicon replacement and, by the paper's own §3 extension, a population of homunculi that implements a human's neural organisation. It does not cover a system whose organisation is merely similar in kind to a conscious one, so it does not license Schwitzgebel's step to the United States ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)). The conclusion is nomological, not metaphysical ("nonreductive functionalism"), and it is a plausibility argument by the author's own account. |
| [LIT-394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-394.md) | Computing Machinery and Intelligence | Turing (1950), Mind 59(236):433–460. "Can machines think?" is replaced by whether a digital computer can play the imitation game so that an interrogator, questioning by teleprinter, identifies it no more reliably than he tells a man from a woman. Universality reduces the question to one computer suitably programmed. Turing predicts that by about 2000 a machine with 10^9 bits of storage will leave an average interrogator no more than a 70 per cent chance of a right identification after five minutes. He answers nine objections, the argument from consciousness by its collapse into solipsism, and proposes reaching the goal by educating a child-machine. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-355](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-355.md)); worth reading as the source of the imitation game and as the first catalogue of objections to machine thought, nine of them, each still argued. Read it for what it actually proposes: not a definition of thinking but the replacement of an ill-posed question by a test, a prediction about 2000 (70 per cent right identification after five minutes, at 10^9 bits), and a programme for reaching it by educating a child-machine. Its reply to the argument from consciousness is an other-minds argument, not a theory of consciousness, and Turing says outright that he does not think there is "no mystery about consciousness". |
| [LIT-395](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-395.md) | The Combination Problem for Panpsychism | Chalmers (2016/2017), in Brüntrup & Jaskolla (eds), Panpsychism: Contemporary Perspectives, OUP, pp. 179–214. How could micro-experiences constitute a macro-subject? The problem splits into subject, quality and structure versions; each yields an argument against constitutive (Russellian) panpsychism, of which the subject-summing and structural mismatch arguments are the strongest. Emergent, autonomous and identity panpsychism avoid combination at a cost in mental causation or physics. Phenomenal bonding, quantum holism, small palettes and informational composition are judged most worth pursuing. No solution is offered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-358](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-358.md)), from the author's posted draft, not the published chapter; worth reading as the map of the combination problem: it splits the problem into subject, quality and structure versions (plus unity, boundary, awareness and grain), turns each into an argument, and sorts every response into emergent, autonomous, identity or combinatorial panpsychism. It solves nothing and says so. Its conclusions are judgements of promise ("phenomenal bonding or quantum holism", "principles of informational composition"), not results. For this record its value is that the subject-summing argument is James's argument against group minds, and that its footnote 7 objects to IIT's exclusion postulate on grounds that have nothing to do with groups. |
| [LIT-397](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-397.md) | Facing Backwards on the Problem of Consciousness | Dennett (1996), Journal of Consciousness Studies 3(1):4–6, a reply to Chalmers's "Facing Up". The easy/hard split is "a major misdirector of attention, an illusion-generator". A vitalist could pose the same "hard problem" of life, and a neuroscientist who set perception aside as hard would have misdescribed vision. Chalmers's reason why consciousness is different repeats the claim. Subtract every function from one's own consciousness and nothing is left but a conviction. Positing experience as fundamental, like mass and charge, needs independent evidence, which is not given ("cutism"). | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-346.md)); worth reading as the three-page statement of the deflationary reply to the hard problem, and as the source of the vitalism, "Crock" and "cutism" analogies. Its one argued point is a challenge, not a refutation: Chalmers owes independent evidence for experience as a fundamental property, the way physics has for mass and charge, and without it the posit does no explanatory work. Its central premise, that once every function is subtracted from one's own consciousness "there is nothing left", is asserted from the author's introspective catalogue. |
| [LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md) | True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works | Dennett (1981; revised 1987, read in Mind Design II, 1997). Belief is "a perfectly objective phenomenon" that can be discerned only by one who adopts the intentional strategy. To be a true believer is to be a system "whose behavior is reliably and voluminously predictable" by it. The choice of stance is free, but its success is objective: Laplacean Martians who skipped it would miss real patterns. Thermostat and person differ only by degree. Why the strategy works is answered easily by evolution, and not yet at all by mechanism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md)), in the revised text reprinted in Mind Design II (1997), not the 1981 printing; worth reading as Dennett's statement that belief is objective although only visible through a strategy: anything whose behaviour is "reliably and voluminously predictable" by the intentional strategy is a believer "in the fullest sense of the word". It turns the 1971 paper's observer-relativity ([LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md)) into "the facts about the success or failure of the stance … are perfectly objective", introduces the Martian thought experiment and the intentional "real patterns" later worked out in [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md), and runs the thermostat-to-person continuum ("no magic moment"). Its criterion admits any system on which the strategy pays, groups included, but the essay never applies it to a group. |
| [LIT-399](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-399.md) | Plain Talk About Neurodevelopmental Epistemology | Minsky (1977), MIT AI Memo 430, also IJCAI-77 pp. 1083–1092. Takes the mind as an organised society of simple "agents", a theory credited to joint work with Papert, and asks how such agents could communicate without language. The proposal: no messages at all, since each argument lives at a fixed location on shared channels ("c-lines") that the agents themselves constitute as short-term memory. A specificity gradient confines low-level agents to local sub-societies, and a case-shift moves an object of attention into a better-described slot. The paper conjectures that these internal cases precede, and shape, the cases of natural language. Openly speculative. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-344.md)); worth reading as the earliest of Minsky's own papers in this record to state the society-of-agents view, then called "The Society of Minds" (Note 1), and as its first worked mechanism: agents communicate by fixed-location channels ("c-lines") instead of messages. It is openly speculative ("a model of scientific irresponsibility", p. 1085), with no data and no program. Read it for the communication scheme, the "specificity gradient", the case-shift mechanism and the conjecture that cognitive cases precede and shape linguistic ones; do not read it as evidence for any of them. That it is the first published statement of the idea is the usual attribution, and this reading could not confirm it (see [NOTE-344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-344.md)). |
| [LIT-400](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-400.md) | Minds, brains, and programs | Searle (1980), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3):417–424. A man who knows no Chinese, locked in a room with rules in English for manipulating Chinese symbols, can answer Chinese questions as well as a native speaker yet understands nothing; so instantiating a program is never by itself sufficient for intentionality ("strong AI" is false). Six replies are answered, the systems reply by letting the man internalise the whole room. Only something with causal powers equivalent to a brain's could think; programs have syntax but no semantics. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-349](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-349.md)); worth reading as the source of the Chinese room and of the six replies (systems, robot, brain simulator, combination, other minds, many mansions) the debate still uses, in Searle's own words. Read it for its scope: the target is "strong AI", the claim that instantiating the right program is by itself sufficient for understanding, and Searle grants that machines, including artifacts with the brain's causal powers, could think. The argument is about understanding and intentionality; consciousness is mentioned, not argued. Its answer to the systems reply (internalise the room) is the part that bears on minds of parts, and it is asserted rather than shown: Searle says the subsystem is "simply a part of" the man, which is what the reply denies. |
| [LIT-401](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-401.md) | What is it like to be a group agent? | List (2016), DOI-10.1111/nous.12162. Group agents (firms, courts, states) are real agents in a thin functionalist sense, and they can have consciousness as awareness. Whether they have phenomenal consciousness depends on which psycho-physical bridge principle is true. Under IIT, List argues informally that a group agent's Φ is low: groups decompose into self-contained units, their steering bodies keep working when partly randomised, and most of their processing happens inside individuals. The exclusion postulate would deny group consciousness even if group Φ were high. So group agents are (close to) not conscious, which List uses to ground a normative asymmetry: groups have only derivative rights. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-340](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-340.md)); the standard reply to [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) from the group-agency side: it grants that organised groups are agents with functional awareness and argues, conditionally on IIT, that they have little or no phenomenal consciousness. Worth reading for its separation of agency from experience and for its three reasons why a group agent's Φ should be low. The low-Φ verdict is argued informally, with no Φ computed for any group, and the paper never answers the reply Schwitzgebel had already made to the objection its third reason restates. |
| [LIT-402](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-402.md) | K-Lines: A Theory of Memory | Minsky (1979/1980), MIT AI Memo 516; Cognitive Science 4(2):117–133. "The function of a memory is to re-create a state of mind." On a memorable event a K-node is made, and its K-line attaches to the agents then active. Reactivated, it re-imposes that partial mental state, but by the level-band principle only on an intermediate band of levels, so the present is seen as an instance of the past without hallucinating the old answer. K-lines attach mainly to earlier K-nodes, forming a K-pyramid against the perceptual P-pyramid, and cross-exclusion lets conflicting details cancel into abstraction. Read from the memo; a programme statement, with no simulation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 from the MIT AI Memo 516 text ([NOTE-352](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-352.md)), not the Cognitive Science version, which was not reachable; worth reading as the society-of-mind programme's theory of memory and the first place Minsky's own text uses the phrase "Society of Mind". The idea to take away is that a memory re-creates a partial mental state rather than retrieving a stored description, and its level-band principle: re-enact only an intermediate band of the original state, so the present problem is seen as an instance of the remembered one. The second half is, by its author's account, not constructive ("from this point, the reader can assume that difficulties in understanding are my fault"), and nothing is simulated or measured. |
| [LIT-403](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-403.md) | Intrinsic content, active memory and the extended mind | Clark (2005), DOI-10.1093/analys/65.1.1. Against Adams & Aizawa: the intrinsic-content objection to [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) fails, because the notion is unclear, silicon parts could carry it, and a conventional encoding linked at run-time to intrinsically contentful states can be a belief's vehicle, inside or outside the head. Against the active-memory objection, the notebook's passivity is a difference below the functional level that matters. The extended mind is a thesis about vehicles. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-363](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-363.md)); worth reading as Clark's first reply to the critics of [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md), and short. It answers Adams and Aizawa's intrinsic-content objection three ways (the notion is unclear, silicon could carry it, and it would not matter), turning their own concession that not every cognitive state needs non-derived content against them; and it answers the "active memory" objection by conceding the notebook is unlike biological memory and arguing that the differences sit below the level a functionalist should attend to. Its replies are parity arguments with imagined cases; it adds no new evidence. It does not engage Rupert ([LIT-422](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-422.md)). |
| [LIT-404](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-404.md) | Does a rock implement every finite-state automaton? | Chalmers (1996), Synthese 108(3):309–333. Putnam's proof that every open system implements every finite-state automaton fails, because implementation needs reliable, counterfactual-supporting transitions for every formal state. Repaired, it survives only for weak formalisms: a clock and a dial implement every inputless FSA, and an input memory and a dial upgrade any system with the right input–output dependencies to every FSA with them. Combinatorial-state automata, whose states are vectors of independently varying components in distinct physical regions, put a strong constraint on implementation. That keeps computation available as a foundation for the theory of mind. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-342.md)), from the author's HTML copy, not the Synthese typeset text; worth reading as the standard reply to Putnam's and Searle's triviality arguments and as the source of the combinatorial-state automaton (CSA). Its result is real but partial: implementation needs counterfactual-supporting transitions over all formal states, inputless FSAs are trivially implemented by any clock plus dial, FSAs with input are implemented by any system with the right input–output dependencies plus an input memory and a dial, and CSAs escape only because a blind implementation must grow by a factor of n per step. Chalmers leaves two open problems (logically possible false implementations, and an overstrict one-region-per-component condition). For this record it decides which formalism a China-brain argument has to be stated in, and it lets one physical system host two minds. |
| [LIT-405](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-405.md) | Where Am I? | Dennett (1978), the closing essay of Brainstorms. A narrator's brain ("Yorick") is kept in a vat in Houston and radio-linked to his body ("Hamlet") under Tulsa. Where is he? Not simply where the body is, and not simply where the brain is: he cannot think "here" of the vat. He favours being wherever his point of view is, finds that unclear, and when the links fail finds himself "in Houston". A computer duplicate ("Hubert") runs in step with Yorick, and either can drive a new body with no detectable switch. The essay ends when the two drift out of step and a second person speaks through the body. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-338.md)), in a retyped course copy, not the printed book; worth reading as the founding thought experiment on where a person is when brain and body are apart, and the place the record's threads on extended vehicles, scattered individuals and functional duplicates meet. It is fiction with a philosophical argument inside it. It tries three answers to "where am I?" (where the body is, where the brain is, where the point of view is), favours the third, admits it is unclear, and ends by showing that two synchronised brains can drift into two persons. It argues by intuition pump and settles nothing; the narrator calls one of its answers a truth "of underwhelming significance". |
| [LIT-406](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-406.md) | Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (1995), Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3):200–219. The "easy" problems of consciousness (discrimination, integration, report, access, attention, control, wakefulness) are problems of explaining functions, and a mechanism that performs a function explains it. The hard problem is that after every such function is explained, "why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?" stays open, so reductive methods cannot answer it. Experience should be taken as fundamental, linked to the physical by psychophysical laws. Two nonbasic candidates are offered, structural coherence (the structure of experience mirrors the structure of awareness) and organizational invariance (fine-grained functional isomorphs have the same experiences), with a speculative double-aspect theory of information as the basic law. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-336.md)); worth reading as the source of the easy/hard distinction, and short. Cite it for three separable things: the hard problem as the claim that explaining every function near experience leaves "why is this accompanied by experience?" open (§§2–3); the outline of a nonreductive theory built from two nonbasic principles, structural coherence and organizational invariance (§7); and the double-aspect theory of information, which the author calls "more of an idea than a theory" (§8). The organizational-invariance argument here is a one-page sketch; the full version is [LIT-392](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-392.md). |
| [LIT-407](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-407.md) | Troubles with Functionalism | Block (1978), Minnesota Studies in the Philosophy of Science 9:261–325. Functionalism ties mental states to the world only through inputs and outputs, so it is "liberal": a body run by a billion people with radios, each implementing one line of your machine table (the nation-of-China system), would be functionally equivalent to you, yet there is prima facie doubt that it has qualia. Putnam's stipulation that no pain-feeler has parts with pain-feeler organisation is an ad hoc patch that fails on its own terms. Psychofunctionalism escapes the doubt for beliefs but perhaps not for qualia, and no specification of inputs and outputs avoids both liberalism and chauvinism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-366](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-366.md)); worth reading as the source of the homunculi-headed robot and the nation-of-China system, and of the first published objection to Putnam's anti-nesting stipulation. Cite it for two things that are easy to run together: the Absent Qualia Argument (a Functional simulation built from people is prima facie without qualia), and the case that Putnam's condition is ad hoc (§1.5). Block grounds the doubt about the China system in its being unlike us psychologically and neurally and designed to mimic us, not in its parts having minds (n. 19). He also grants that a Psychofunctional homunculi-head could have beliefs (§2.1). So it is not a source for "a whole made of minded parts cannot be conscious". |
| [LIT-408](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-408.md) | Jokes and the Logic of the Cognitive Unconscious | Minsky (1980), MIT AI Memo 603; in Vaina & Hintikka (eds.), Cognitive Constraints on Communication (Reidel, 1984), pp. 175–200. Commonsense logic cannot be made reliable, so each mind accumulates "censors" that learn the precursors of known-bad thought (paradox, circling, false analogy) and suppress it before it occurs. On that view, humour is censor-learning. Its common element is an "unexpected frame-substitution", and laughter both stops the absurd line of thought and holds it in focus. Logical nonsense is then as "naughty" as Freud's forbidden wishes, which removes the gap in Freud's theory. An essay with no data or program. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 from the MIT AI Memo 603 text ([NOTE-361](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-361.md)), not the 1984 book chapter, which was not reachable; worth reading as the society-of-mind programme's account of humour and of "negative meta-knowledge". Its argument is that commonsense reasoning cannot be made reliable, so minds learn "censors" that suppress known-bad lines of thought, and that humour and laughter are how those censors are taught and engaged, which dissolves Freud's puzzle about nonsense jokes. It is an essay: no data, no program, and its evolutionary story is offered as "no plea for this particular scenario". |
| [LIT-409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-409.md) | How a materialist can deny that the United States is probably conscious – response to Schwitzgebel | Kammerer (2015), DOI-10.1007/s11406-015-9653-z. A short reply to [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) proposing the Sophisticated Anti-Nesting Principle (SAP). A whole W that has a functional property P normally sufficient for a conscious state S lacks S when some part of W plays a role that (A) requires the part to have conscious states representing W and (B) is indispensable: without some part playing such a role, W would lack P. The SAP keeps Schwitzgebel's antheads and Block's tiny-people neurons conscious, admits some group consciousness, and denies it to the US, whose citizens represent the US and could not be replaced by parts that do not. It is justified by an Occam-style rule against ascribing consciousness where other subjects' states explain the behaviour. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-362](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-362.md)); the most careful anti-nesting principle in the record, and the one aimed directly at [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md). Worth reading because it draws the line that matters for the society-of-mind bridge: a whole is denied a conscious state only when the functional organisation that would ground it runs through parts that consciously represent the whole and could not be replaced by parts that do not. Its application to the United States rests on an asserted counterfactual, and its justification is an Occam-style principle the author says needs further work. Schwitzgebel replied in Philosophia 44 (2016). |
| [LIT-410](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-410.md) | A Framework for Representing Knowledge | Minsky (1974), MIT AI Memo 306. A self-declared partial theory of thinking: on meeting a situation one retrieves a frame, a stereotyped structure whose terminals carry conditions and weakly bound default assignments, and adapts it by replacing details. Frames that share terminals form frame-systems whose transformations stand for moves, actions or changes of viewpoint, and failed matches are routed through a learned similarity network. The memo applies this to vision, imagery, language, memory and problem solving, and ends by arguing that consistency-seeking logical systems cannot represent commonsense knowledge, because they are monotonic. Nothing is implemented or tested. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-337](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-337.md)); worth reading as the source of the frame idea and of the critique of "logistic" representation that later motivated non-monotonic reasoning. It is a proposal, not a result: no program is described as built, nothing is measured, and the author says so ("Apology!", p. 2). The parts to take away are the frame with weakly bound default assignments (§1.11), frame-systems sharing terminals across viewpoints (§1), terminals read as questions (§2.8), the similarity network with cluster "capitols" as an account of family resemblance (§§3.4–3.5), and the appendix on monotonicity and consistency (§6). It contains no society-of-agents idea; that arrives in Plain Talk ([LIT-399](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-399.md)), which calls itself in part a sequel to this memo. |
| [LIT-411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-411.md) | Could a Large Language Model be Conscious? | Chalmers (2023), arXiv:2303.07103; Boston Review, 9 August 2023; from a NeurIPS 2022 invited talk. Asks for a feature X that LLMs have (or lack) and that indicates consciousness (or its absence). Self-report, seeming-conscious, conversation and general intelligence give at most weak evidence for it. Biology, senses and embodiment, world and self models, recurrent processing, a global workspace and unified agency are the evidence against. All but biology are temporary. On mainstream assumptions: under 10% credence for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade. Twelve challenges are offered as roadmap or red flags. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md)), from arXiv v3 (the Boston Review text), with v1's conclusions compared; worth reading as the clearest short statement of the case for and against consciousness in LLMs, and as the origin of the "theory-balanced" credence approach that Butlin et al. built on. Its method is a regimented request for a feature X, and its verdicts are credences offered "for illustrative purposes": under 10% for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade, on "mainstream assumptions". It does not break the deadlock [THEORY-023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-023.md) describes. It is an instance of it: mimicry undercuts self-report, the main obstacles are theory-derived, and biology is set aside rather than answered. |
| [LIT-414](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-414.md) | High-level perception, representation, and analogy: A critique of artificial intelligence methodology | Chalmers, French & Hofstadter (1992), DOI-10.1080/09528139208953747. Traditional AI hands its programs representations built by people who already know the answer, so models like BACON (Kepler's third law) and the Structure-Mapping Engine (atom and solar system) skip the hard part, high-level perception: deciding what is relevant and how to organise it. Nor can the gap be filled later by a separate "representation module", because analogy shapes perception and the task decides which representation is right. Copycat, in a microdomain of letter strings, is offered as an architecture that builds representations and mappings together. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-359](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-359.md)), from the authors' preprint (CRCC Technical Report 49, March 1991) that Chalmers posts; the published text was not seen. Worth reading as the clearest short statement of the Fluid Analogies Research Group's case against hand-coded representations, and as the most accessible description of Copycat. It is an argument, not a result: its two arguments against a separate "representation module" are informal and good, its case studies (BACON, SME) are fair as far as they go, and the evidence it offers for Copycat is a description of the architecture and one worked problem, with nothing measured in the paper itself. |
| [LIT-415](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-415.md) | Extended Cognition and Extended Consciousness | Chalmers (2019), DOI-10.1093/oso/9780190662813.003.0002. The 1998 extended-mind thesis as stated is too weak, since opponents accept extension in wired-in "extended circuit" cases. The interesting thesis is that mental states can be partly constituted by external entities in virtue of the subject's sensorimotor interaction with them. Consciousness does not extend this way, on the proposal that it requires information directly available for global control, and perceptually mediated availability is indirect. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-356](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-356.md)); worth reading as Chalmers's own later statement of what the extended-mind thesis of [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) is and where it stops. It does two things. It replaces the 1998 paper's implicit thesis, which it concedes is too weak because even the critics accept it for wired-in "extended circuit" cases, with one that requires constitution "in virtue of the subject's sensorimotor interaction" (§1). And it argues that consciousness does not extend, because consciousness needs information directly available for global control and perception makes availability indirect (§3). Both are proposals, argued in a short chapter: the thesis is offered as "extensionally correct", and the directness account is offered as an explanation of why there are no plausible cases, not as a knockdown. |
| [LIT-421](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-421.md) | Foreword | Chalmers (2008), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195333213.002.0007. The co-author's retrospective on the extended mind: his iPhone is "part of my mind already". The one principled objection is that perception and action bound the mental. His reply is revisionist and contextualist: whether Otto's belief counts as extended flips with explanatory purpose. No Otto-style twin case works for consciousness, so he tentatively keeps an internal conscious core. The thesis needs only a weak, parity-style functionalism and is compatible with dualism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-369](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-369.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of where Chalmers stands on the thesis he co-authored, ten years on. Three things in eight pages: the iPhone as a present-day Otto's notebook; the perception-action boundary as the one principled objection, answered by explanatory revisionism and a "Necker cube" view on which whether Otto's belief is extended depends on explanatory purpose; and a tentative internal "conscious core", resting on the failure of any Otto-style twin case for consciousness. It is a foreword: every position is stated briefly and several are offered as "perhaps". |
| [LIT-422](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-422.md) | Challenges to the Hypothesis of Extended Cognition | Rupert (2004), DOI-10.5840/jphil2004101826. The embedded hypothesis (HEMC: cognition leans heavily on external props, but is the organism's) competes with the extended one (HEC), and conservatism favours HEMC unless HEC buys explanatory power. It does not. [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md)'s criteria either make phone directories into beliefs or privilege the organism, and memory research (interference, the generation effect, conversation) shows internal and external storage are different kinds. A generic kind covering both does no work. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-343](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-343.md)), in the author's pre-publication version; worth reading as the case that a conservative "embedded" hypothesis explains everything the extended hypothesis does, and as the empirical version of the critique. Its two arguments: a dilemma on [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md)'s past-endorsement criterion (keep it and the organism is privileged after all; drop it and directory assistance gives Otto beliefs about every listed phone number), and memory research (interference, the generation effect, conversation) showing internal and external storage behave as different kinds, so that a kind covering both does no explanatory work. Its strength is that it argues from cognitive science rather than intuition; its limit is that the empirical differences are about fine-grained profiles, which a defender can accept and still claim a coarse kind. |
| [LIT-425](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-425.md) | The Meta-Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (2018), Journal of Consciousness Studies 25(9–10):6–61. The meta-problem is to explain, in terms that do not mention consciousness, why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem. It is an "easy" problem with an empirical programme. Of thirteen candidate mechanisms, the most promising is an introspective model that attributes primitive relations of awareness to primitive qualities, with a sense of acquaintance. A realist theory should explain how its basis of consciousness produces these judgments, which IIT and biological theories struggle to do. Debunking arguments for illusionism can be blocked, but a residual sense of coincidence remains. Only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, and it is false because people feel pain. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-354](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-354.md)); worth reading as the statement of the meta-problem, explaining in topic-neutral terms why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem, and as a survey of thirteen candidate mechanisms. Cite it for four things: the meta-problem as an "easy" problem with a research programme; the meta-problem challenge to theories of consciousness, which tells against IIT and biological theories; the analysis of debunking and coincidence arguments for illusionism; and the argument that only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, with a Moorean rejection of strong illusionism. Its own preferred solution is offered as "closer to a fleshed-out explanandum" than an explanation. |
| [LIT-427](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-427.md) | Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning | Selfridge (1959), Mechanisation of Thought Processes Vol. I (HMSO), pp. 513–526 plus discussion to p. 531. Pattern recognition by a "pandemonium": data demons hold the input, computational subdemons compute features, each cognitive demon "shrieks" a weighted sum of them, and a decision demon picks the loudest. The system learns by hill-climbing on the weights and by "natural selection" on the subdemons, culling those of low worth and breeding new ones by mutation and by "conjugation" of pairs. It is applied to telling dots from dashes in hand-keyed Morse. In the discussion McCarthy proposes reading the demons' private computation as unconscious and their public shouting as conscious thought. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-360](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-360.md)); worth reading as the first published architecture of a mind-like process built from many quasi-independent "demons", each doing one narrow job, with no part holding the whole's competence. That is the decomposition template that Minsky's agents inherit. Cite it as an engineering proposal with a preliminary result reported only in discussion, not as a theory of mind. Its one remark on consciousness is McCarthy's, in the discussion, and it is an aside. |
| [LIT-431](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-431.md) | Time and the Observer: The Where and When of Consciousness in the Brain | Dennett & Kinsbourne (1992), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 15(2):183–201, with open peer commentary. There is no place in the brain where "it all comes together" for consciousness. Discriminations are made once, locally, and revised in parallel "drafts", none canonical. The brain represents temporal order by content, not by the timing of its own vehicles, as a dated letter does. Colour phi, the cutaneous rabbit and Libet's timing results stop looking anomalous. Whether a revision was pre-experiential (Stalinesque) or post-experiential (Orwellian) has no answer at that scale. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-367](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-367.md)), the target article only; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Multiple Drafts model and of the case against "Cartesian materialism", worked out on four timing phenomena (colour phi, the cutaneous rabbit, Libet's backward referral and his delayed intention). Its sound core is the distinction between the time a content is represented and the time it represents. Its strong claim, that the Orwellian/Stalinesque distinction "need have no answer" below a few hundred milliseconds, is an argument from indistinguishability, not a demonstration. The open peer commentary (pp. 201–247) was not read. |
| [LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md) | The Emotion Machine: Commonsense Thinking, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of the Human Mind | Minsky (2006), Simon & Schuster, read in the author's 2005 draft. Emotions are Ways to Think, not a separate faculty. Each emotional state turns some mental resources on and others off, by Selectors that Critics trigger when they recognise a type of problem. The same machinery serves ordinary thinking. The book adds six levels of mental activity, from instinctive reaction to self-conscious reflection. It treats "consciousness", "emotion" and "pain" as suitcase words for many processes, and the Self as a network of partial self-models. It is a design argued from examples. Against Damasio, it treats the body as one more resource the brain uses, not the stuff of emotion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 in the author's posted draft of 2005 ([NOTE-348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-348.md)), not in the published book; worth reading as the late, fullest statement of the Society of Mind programme. It is the one where emotion is put inside thinking: an emotional state is a selection of mental resources switched on and off, made by Selectors that Critics trigger, and so it is a Way to Think. Read it as a design proposal argued by examples, not as evidence. It reports no experiment, Minsky labels several of its central ideas his own conjectures, and it sets the body to the side of emotion, against the bodily account of Damasio ([LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md)) that this record holds. |
| [LIT-433](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-433.md) | Quining Qualia | Dennett (1988), in Marcel & Bisiach (eds.), Consciousness in Contemporary Science, OUP, pp. 42–77. Qualia as tradition has them are ineffable, intrinsic, private and directly apprehensible, and fifteen intuition pumps argue that nothing has all four. Two neurosurgical routes to an apparent colour inversion, one changing qualia and one only memory-linked reactions, feel the same from the inside. So the subject cannot know his own qualia better than an outside tester can. What is real is practical ineffability and idiosyncrasy: we refer to information-rich public properties through our own detectors of them. Hence "there simply are no qualia at all". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-357](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-357.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of qualia eliminativism and the source of the post-Cartesian side in the record's consciousness readings. It argues by fifteen intuition pumps, not by proof, and says so. Its lasting results are two: the alternative-neurosurgery and Chase-and-Sanborn cases, which show that neither the subject nor the physiologist can separate a change in qualia from a change in reactions to them; and a positive account of practical ineffability and privacy as idiosyncratic, information-rich property detection. Its conclusion, "there simply are no qualia at all", is a tactical choice of words by the author's own endnote 2, not a stronger thesis than that. |
| [LIT-436](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-436.md) | Intelligence without representation | Brooks (1991), Artificial Intelligence 47:139–159, written in 1987. Argues that AI should be built incrementally from complete autonomous "Creatures" tested in the real world, and that the system should be decomposed by activity into parallel layers, each connecting sensing to action, not by function into perception, a central reasoner and action. His robots have no central representation and no central control: each layer is a fixed network of simple finite-state machines, and a higher layer subsumes a lower one by suppressing or inhibiting its wires. Coherent behaviour emerges, "in the eye of an observer", from competing behaviours. Hypothesis: representation is the wrong unit of abstraction for the bulk of intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md)) from the copy Brooks posts; worth reading as the decomposition side built and run: a robot whose purposive behaviour comes from parallel layers of simple finite-state machines with no central representation and no central control, which Brooks likens to Minsky's account of human behaviour. The coherence of the whole, he says, exists "in the eye of an observer". The evidence is three layers on one physical robot, described rather than measured. It makes no claim about minds or experience and disclaims interest in the philosophy. |
| [LIT-438](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-438.md) | The bounds of cognition | Adams & Aizawa (2001), DOI-10.1080/09515080120033571. Against [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md), Dennett, Donald and Hutchins: cognition has two necessary marks, non-derived content and a kind of causal processing found in brains. Notebooks, screens and tools have only derived content and work by different processes, so actual cognition is brain-bound as a contingent fact. Causal coupling does not extend a process, and brain-plus-tool systems are too motley for a science. They grant the parity principle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-368](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-368.md)); worth reading as the first sustained reply to [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) and the source of the "mark of the cognitive" line of criticism. It grants parity and argues that cognition has two necessary marks, non-derived content and a distinctive kind of causal process, which notebooks, screens and tools lack as a matter of contingent fact; and that brain-plus-tool systems are too motley to support a science. Read it for that structure, not for proofs: both marks are assumed ("we assume without argument"), and the processing differences it lists are asserted from common knowledge, not measured. The phrase "coupling-constitution fallacy" is not in this paper; it comes from the authors' later work. |
| [LIT-439](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-439.md) | The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition | Levin (2019), Frontiers in Psychology 10:2688. Proposes "Scale-Free Cognition": an Individual or Self is the set of parts that pursue a goal together, bounded by the farthest events in space and time it can measure and try to change (its "cognitive light cone"). Selves scale up from homeostatic loops through memory and anticipation, and cells merge into larger Selves by sharing bioelectric state through gap junctions; cancer is the boundary shrinking back to one cell. Because every level that pursues its own goal is a Self, most living systems hold many nested, coexisting Selves, "not one, as implied by Integrated Information Theory". Levin's "Self" is a goal-pursuing collective, an agent and an individual in this record's terms; the essay gives no account of a self as subject. A hypothesis essay: no model and no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-341.md)); worth reading as the composition-side statement that agency is nested by default: a Self is whatever set of parts pursues a goal together, so cells, organs, organisms and swarms are Selves at once, each bounded by its "cognitive light cone". It is a hypothesis-and-theory essay with no model, no measurement procedure for the light cone and no data of its own. Its one sentence against IIT's single-Self picture is asserted in a bracket, not argued, and its consciousness claims are confined to a closing speculation. |
| [LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md) | Intentional Systems | Dennett (1971), Journal of Philosophy 68(4):87–106. An Intentional system is one whose behaviour can be explained and predicted by ascribing beliefs and desires and assuming rationality, which is the Intentional stance beside the design and physical stances. Being one is relative to an observer's strategy, and the choice of stance is pragmatic. The stance is "unmetaphysical": it sets aside composition, consciousness and moral standing. As psychology it is vacuous, because it presupposes rationality. Any theory that gives content to a part takes out a "loan of intelligence", repayable only by analysing away the part's reader: "there a little man is concealed". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-350](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-350.md)); worth reading as the first statement in print of the intentional stance and of the homunculus debt that Dennett later answers with "discharge". Its definition makes being an Intentional system relative to an observer's predictive strategy, and it says outright that the definition "does not say that Intentional systems really have beliefs and desires" (p. 91). True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)) later withdraws exactly that relativity. Its lasting tool for this record is the "loan of intelligence" (p. 96): any theory that gives a part content owes an account of that part's reader, and "wherever a theory relies on a formulation bearing the logical marks of Intentionality, there a little man is concealed". The paper does not treat a group as an Intentional system. |
| [LIT-442](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-442.md) | The Self as a Center of Narrative Gravity | Dennett (1992), in Kessel, Cole & Johnson (eds.), Self and Consciousness: Multiple Perspectives, Erlbaum. A self is an abstractum, "a theorist's fiction", like a centre of gravity: no part of the brain, but a well-behaved posit of interpretation. It is like a fictional character, indeterminate beyond what its "text" fixes, and a selfless process can produce one (a novel-writing robot whose story is true of it). Brains are bundles of partly autonomous systems that make themselves cohere into one autobiography; when the story coheres around two points, there are two selves. Read in a copy-edited transcription. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-364](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-364.md)), in a third party's copy-edited transcription of the text Dennett posted, not in the Erlbaum printing; worth reading as the short, canonical statement that a self is an abstractum, a "theorist's fiction" of the same kind as a centre of gravity, posited by interpretation around which a life's narrative coheres. Read it as an analogy and two thought experiments (the novel-writing robot "Gilbert", the Updike sequel), not as an argument from evidence. Its evolutionary story of self-talk is labelled speculation, and its empirical support (Gazzaniga's split-brain work, multiple personality cases) is cited, not shown. |
| [LIT-444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-444.md) | Examining the Society of Mind | Singh (2003), Computing and Informatics 22(6):521–543. A sympathetic exposition of Minsky's Society of Mind by his student. It traces the theory's history: Minsky and Papert's 1970s copy-demo robot, the procedure-bearing frames of 1974, the abandoned 1976 book drafts, and the 1977 and 1980 papers. It catalogues the mechanisms and how agents communicate without shared symbols. It finds resemblances in Bayes nets, case-based reasoning, blackboards, Cyc, Soar and multiagent systems, none of which it calls a Society of Mind. Its verdict is that the theory has never been implemented. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-339.md)); worth reading as the shortest reliable map of The Society of Mind ([LIT-429](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-429.md)), written by the student who worked with Minsky on its sequel. It gives the theory's history from the 1970s memos, a catalogue of its mechanisms (agents and agencies, K-lines, nemes and nomes, frames and transframes, difference-engines, censors, A- and B-brains, ways agents communicate and grow), and a survey of later AI it resembles. It is an exposition, not a test: it reports no implementation and quotes the theory more than it argues for it. Its history leans on unpublished 1976 drafts that only the author saw. |
| [LIT-445](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-445.md) | From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0 | Oizumi, Albantakis & Tononi (2014), PLoS Computational Biology 10(5):e1003588. IIT 3.0 states five axioms of experience (existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion), turns each into a postulate about mechanisms in a state, and identifies an experience with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a "complex". Exclusion makes a complex a local maximum of integrated conceptual information Φ over all overlapping sets of elements, so complexes cannot overlap and no subset or superset of a complex is conscious. Worked logic-gate examples show minor complexes beside a major one, an inactive network that is conscious, a minimally conscious photodiode, and a feed-forward "zombie" functionally equivalent to a conscious system. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md)), equations excepted; worth reading as the formal statement of the exclusion postulate that Schwitzgebel's 2014 manuscript ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)) attacks: "of all overlapping sets of elements, only one set can be conscious", a complex being a local maximum of Φ against every overlapping set. It is IIT's anti-nesting principle, stated as a postulate and motivated only by the phenomenological exclusion axiom; the paper's Occam's-razor argument is given for exclusion within a mechanism, not between systems. It also says plainly that function does not fix consciousness, which is IIT's answer to whether agency built from parts brings experience with it. |
| [LIT-446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-446.md) | Survival and Identity | Lewis (1976), DOI-10.1525/9780520353060-002. What matters in survival is mental continuity and connectedness (the R-relation among person-stages), and it is also identity, because the two answers relate different things. Persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the I-relation (being stages of one person) is the R-relation in every possible case. Fission and fusion are two persons sharing stages, counted as one by "tensed identity"; Methuselah is a continuum of overlapping 137-year persons; degrees of personal identity come from supervaluating over cut-offs for R. Against Perry: two persons, not three, took part in a fission. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md)), from a scan of the 1976 printing posted on Andrew M. Bailey's "Papers by David Lewis" page, OCR'd here; worth reading as the four-dimensionalist reconciliation of Parfit with common sense, and the source of stage-sharing and counting by tensed identity. It agrees with Parfit that what matters is mental continuity and connectedness, the R-relation among person-stages, and denies that this conflicts with identity: persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the relation of being stages of one person is the R-relation. Fission becomes two persons sharing their early stages, and degrees are handled by supervaluation. A reconciliation by redefinition of counting, which Lewis grants is "somewhat counterintuitive". |
| [LIT-447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-447.md) | Personal Identity | Parfit (1971), DOI-10.2307/2184309. Against two beliefs, that every question about personal identity must have an answer and that important questions turn on it. In Wiggins's division case, each half-brain recipient stands in the relation that would be survival if there were only one, so "how could a double success be a failure?". What matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity is one-one and all-or-nothing. Q-memory and q-intention show the relations need not presuppose identity. Speaking of past and future selves by degree of connectedness, the principle of self-interest has no independent force. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Athens course page; worth reading as the paper that separated what matters in survival from identity, and the short original of Part III of Reasons and Persons. Its division case makes "I survive as neither" absurd and "I survive as both" incompatible with identity, so it concludes that what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity cannot. It supplies q-memory, the non-branching criterion, and the vocabulary of successive selves. Its first conclusion is argued; its claim that connectedness matters more than continuity is left, in its own words, needing "more arguments than I have space to give". |
| [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md) | Self models | Metzinger (2007, rev. 2013), Scholarpedia 2(10):4174. There is no substantial self, only a phenomenal self-model (PSM): the conscious part of an organism's self-model, an instrument of global control. A phenomenal self arises "if and only if a system operates under a transparent PSM", one it cannot introspectively recognise as a model; a first-person perspective is a transparent model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Self-models can be unconscious and artificial, as in Bongard, Zykov and Lipson's limping starfish robot; embodiment comes in three orders, the third conscious. Full-body illusions are offered as the experimental handle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-372](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-372.md)); worth reading as Metzinger's own short, open statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT) behind Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)): there is no self, only a phenomenal self-model, and a system experiences itself as a self when that model is transparent, that is, when it cannot introspectively recognise it as a model. It is an encyclopedia article, not an argument: the central claim is stated as a definition with a prediction attached, its empirical examples are cited, and the online text is a revision later than the 2007 acceptance, with editing slips. |
| [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md) | Of Personal Identity | Hume (1739), Treatise 1.4.6, with the Appendix (1740). There is no impression of a self, "constant and invariable", so no idea of one: introspection finds only "some particular perception or other", and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". The identity we ascribe to it is "fictitious", like that of plants, ships and churches: an easy transition of the imagination along resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it, so that hard cases are "grammatical" rather than philosophical.
