Zero-shot (probe trained on ID data, OOD only for selecting the layer), it beats retraining the last layer, sharply under subpopulation shift. Layer L − 2 beats L − 1 in every dataset shown. A distance-ratio sensitivity score finds intermediate features less displaced by the shift than penultimate ones, most of all for minority groups. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-541](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-541.md)); worth reading as the measurement that, under distribution shift, a trained classifier's best linear probe is usually not on the penultimate layer: Intermediate Layer Classifiers (linear probes on frozen layer-l features, l ≤ L − 2) beat last-layer retraining in the few-shot setting on most of nine shifted datasets, and, trained only on in-distribution data, raise worst-group accuracy from 79.4% to 87.1% on Waterbirds and 56.0% to 82.0% on CelebA. The proposed reason is that penultimate features move further under shift, especially for minority groups, while intermediate ones stay put. Selection of the layer uses OOD validation data, and the gains for ViTs are small. |
| [LIT-679](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-679.md) | A Random Matrix Analysis of Random Fourier Features: Beyond the Gaussian Kernel, a Precise Phase Transition, and the Corresponding Double Descent | Liao, Couillet & Mahoney (2020), NeurIPS 2020 and J. Stat. Mech. (2021). For random Fourier features ΣX = [cos(WX); sin(WX)] with n, p, N large and comparable, the expected resolvent of ΣXᵀΣX/n is asymptotically Q̄ = ((N/n)(Kcos/(1+δcos) + Ksin/(1+δsin)) + λI)⁻¹, with δσ = (1/n)tr KσQ̄, not the Gaussian-kernel prediction. Closed forms for training and test MSE follow and match MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and Kannada-MNIST. In the ridgeless limit the δ jump at 2N = n, separating an under- and an over-parameterized phase; the test MSE diverges there unless test data sit within about λ of the training data, which is the double-descent peak. A tuned λ removes it. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-519](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-519.md)); worth reading as an exact random-matrix account of double descent in random Fourier feature ridge regression when n, p and N are large together: the RFF Gram matrix does not converge to the Gaussian kernel in spectral norm, but its resolvent has a deterministic equivalent built from the cos and sin kernels with corrections δcos, δsin solving a fixed point (Theorem 1). Training and test MSE follow in closed form (Theorems 2–3). As λ → 0 the δ jump from O(1) to order 1/λ across 2N = n, so the model has two phases, and the test error diverges at the boundary when test data differ from training data; that singularity is the double-descent peak. Data need only be concentrated random vectors, not Gaussian. |
| [LIT-680](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-680.md) | Proving Linear Mode Connectivity of Neural Networks via Optimal Transport | Ferbach, Goujaud, Gidel & Dieuleveut (2024), AISTATS 2024. Finding the permutation that aligns two networks' neurons layer by layer is an optimal-transport problem between empirical weight distributions, so Wasserstein convergence rates bound when the permuted straight line stays low-loss. Wide two-layer nets trained by SGD in the mean-field regime are linearly connected modulo permutation with high probability. Deep nets with i.i.d. neuron weights (as at initialization) are too, once each layer is wider than about (1/ε) to the power of the previous one, a rate shown tight. Low-dimensional weight distributions need less width, and a covariance-weighted weight matching beats plain weight matching. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-543](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-543.md)); the first proof of linear mode connectivity modulo permutation beyond a single hidden layer. Aligning neurons is an optimal-transport problem between the empirical distributions of their weights, so convergence rates of empirical measures in Wasserstein distance bound how wide a network must be for the permuted straight line to stay low-loss. It proves the result for wide two-layer nets trained by SGD in the mean-field regime, and for deep nets whenever neuron weights within a layer are i.i.d., which holds at initialization. The width needed grows like (1/ε) to the power of the previous layer's width, a rate shown to be tight, and falls if weights concentrate near a low-dimensional subspace. The proofs rest on independence of neurons, which the authors call the central and least realistic assumption. |
| [LIT-681](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-681.md) | Optimizing Mode Connectivity for Class Incremental Learning | Wen, Cheng, Qiu, Wang, Pan & Li (2023), ICML 2023. In class-incremental learning the linear path between adjacent continual minima crosses a high-loss ridge for earlier tasks. OPC finds a curved low-loss path, modelled as the line plus a layer-wise Fourier-series perturbation, with the path loss split at a switching point between old-task and new-task memory losses. EOPC averages points in a cylinder around the switching point and is added as post-processing to existing methods, improving PODNet and AANet on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet-1K and sharply reducing forgetting. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-524](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-524.md)); worth reading as the class-incremental counterpart of Mirzadeh et al.: between adjacent continual minima in class-incremental learning, the straight line crosses a high-loss ridge for the earlier tasks, and a curved path avoids it. OPC parameterises that path as the line plus a layer-wise Fourier perturbation that vanishes at both ends (2 × 96 × 4 learned numbers for a 96-layer ResNet), splits the path loss at a switching point into old-task and new-task halves, and pushes it to flat regions by sampling a cylinder around it. Averaging points near the switching point (EOPC) adds 0.3 to 5.1 points of average incremental accuracy to PODNet and AANet on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet-1K. In Table 4 it beats Bezier and simplex paths only on the longer task sequences. |
| [LIT-682](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-682.md) | Exploring Neural Network Landscapes: Star-Shaped and Geodesic Connectivity | Lin, Li & Wu (2024), preprint. For a two-layer ReLU student of an orthonormal teacher, and for deep linear networks, over-parameterisation makes any two global minima two-piece linearly connected and gives any finite set of minima a common centre linearly connected to each (star- shaped connectivity). Under a sparsity bias like SGD's, the shortest path on the minimum manifold is nearly as short as the straight line, with normalised geodesic distance ≤ 1 + c₂/(r√m). A centre-finding objective locates such centres for independently trained FNNs, VGG16 and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10, with no permutation alignment. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-535](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-535.md)); worth reading as the theory of star-shaped connectivity without permutations. For a two-layer ReLU student of an orthonormal teacher, and for deep linear networks, sufficiently wide networks have any two minima joined by a two-piece linear path and any finite set of minima linearly joined to a common centre on the minimum manifold. SGD's bias toward sparse solutions explains why the shortest path on the manifold is nearly as short as the straight line (normalised geodesic distance ≤ 1 + c₂/(r√m)). Experiments find centres for three to five independently trained FNNs, VGG16s and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10 with almost no barrier. Preprint. |
| [LIT-683](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-683.md) | Exact expressions for double descent and implicit regularization via surrogate random design | Dereziński, Liang & Mahoney (2019), NeurIPS 2020. For the Moore–Penrose estimator X⁺y in linear regression, a determinantal surrogate design (density ∝ pdet(XXᵀ), Poisson sample size with mean n) gives exact MSE: σ² tr((Σ + λnI)⁻¹)(1 − αn)/(d − n) + w*ᵀ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹w*·(d − n)/tr((Σ + λnI)⁻¹) for n < d, σ² tr(Σ⁻¹) at n = d, σ² tr(Σ⁻¹)(1 − βn)/(n − d) for n > d, where n = tr(Σ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹). For n < d, E[X⁺y] equals the population ridge solution with that λn: over-parameterization is implicit ridge regularization whose strength makes n the effective dimension. The surrogate agrees with the i.i.d. design as d, n → ∞ for sub-Gaussian data. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-518](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-518.md)); worth reading as the exact, non-asymptotic account of double descent and implicit regularization for minimum-norm least squares: replacing the i.i.d. design by a determinantal "surrogate" design gives closed-form MSE in every regime (Theorem 1) and shows that, below the interpolation threshold n < d, the expected minimum-norm solution equals the population ridge solution with the λn for which the ridge effective dimension tr(Σ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹) equals n (Theorem 2). The surrogate matches the i.i.d. design asymptotically for sub-Gaussian data (Theorem 3), at an empirically O(1/d) rate. The tool is a class of random matrices for which determinant and expectation commute. |
| [LIT-689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-689.md) | Stories and the Meaning of Life | Fischer (2009), Philosophic Exchange 39(1), pp. 3–15. Section I sketches his framework for moral responsibility: guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; it consists in acting from one's own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism; responsibility is historical and compatible with causal determinism; and the moral of Frankfurt-style cases is that it depends on how the actual sequence unfolds. The paper's thesis is that the value of acting freely is the value of artistic self-expression: free action makes a life a story with narrative value, though the life is judged mainly by moral and prudential standards. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-547](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-547.md)); worth reading as the only first-hand, lawful statement by Fischer that the record holds of his framework for moral responsibility: guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; guidance control is mechanism ownership plus moderate reasons-responsiveness; responsibility is historical and compatible with causal determinism; and the moral of Frankfurt-style cases is that responsibility depends on the actual sequence. Its own thesis is that the value of acting freely is the value of artistic self-expression, which gives a life narrative value. It lists the framework's elements without arguing for them. |
| [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md) | Moral Responsibility | Talbert (2019; revised 2024), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. A survey of moral responsibility: its relation to free will and determinism, forward-looking, Strawsonian and reasons-responsiveness accounts, the attributability/accountability distinction that grew from Wolf and Watson, the moral competence condition (Wolf's JoJo), conversational views, standing to blame, outcomes, skepticism, moral luck, ultimate responsibility, manipulation and the epistemic condition. Its §2.3 is a page-referenced summary of Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-548.md)); worth reading as the record's map of moral responsibility apart from the free-will question, and as its most exact second-hand source for two accounts the record cannot read first-hand: Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control (§2.3, with page references to the 1998 book) and Wolf's critique of Real Self views and her moral-competence condition, including the JoJo case (§§3.1.1, 3.2). It reports Wolf's praise/blame asymmetry only in one sentence of its preamble. |
| [LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Frankfurt (1971), The Journal of Philosophy 68(1):5–20. What is essential to a person is the structure of the will. A person's will is the effective first-order desire, the one that moves him "all the way to action" (p. 8). A second-order volition is wanting a desire to be one's will; persons have them, and wantons, who "do not care" about their wills, do not (pp. 10–11). Forming one is identifying with one desire and withdrawing from another (p. 13). Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, "securing the conformity of his will to his second-order volitions" (p. 15), and a decisive identification "resounds" through all higher orders (p. 16). Moral responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts "of his own free will" (pp. 18–20). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md)); worth reading as the source of the hierarchical account of the will, which the record has so far held only second-hand: first- and second-order desires, the will as the effective desire, second-order volitions, wantons and persons, freedom of the will as having the will one wants, decisive identification that "resounds" through higher orders, and a responsibility that needs neither a free will nor alternatives. Read it knowing that it is short and programmatic, that identification is stated, not analysed, and that it already contains both the decisive commitment (p. 16) and the acceptance of an addict made by another (n. 10), which the record's surveys date later. |
| [LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt (1969), The Journal of Philosophy 66(23):829–839. The principle of alternate possibilities (PAP), "a person is morally responsible for what he has done only if he could have done otherwise", is false. Coercion excuses only when the agent acts because of it (§§II– III). Black, ready to make Jones4 act as he wants and never needing to, shows that circumstances can make an action unavoidable without playing any role in bringing it about (§IV); such a fact "does not help in any way to understand" the action and cannot excuse it (§V). PAP should be replaced by: not responsible "if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise", which "does not appear to conflict" with compatibilism (pp. 838–839). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md)); worth reading as the origin of Frankfurt-style cases and the shortest first-hand statement of the argument against the principle of alternate possibilities: a fact that makes an action unavoidable but plays no role in bringing it about cannot excuse, so PAP should give way to "a person is not morally responsible for what he has done if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise" (p. 838). Read it knowing that its case is schematic (Black, Jones4 and "a certain action"; the voting and shooting versions in the record's surveys are later retellings), that its prior sign is in a footnote, and that it leaves "could have done otherwise" and "morally responsible" unanalysed on purpose (n. 1). |
